opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the difficulty comes from a few different places. When you do blind locomotion, the robot only relies on proprioception: joint positions, velocities, the IMU, maybe the history of those. And it turns out you can get surprisingly far with that. The robot learns to feel the ground and react, so it can walk over rough terrain and even climb small steps just by bumping into them and adapting.

But once you want to do something more dynamic, like climbing high steps, jumping over gaps, or walking through stairs at speed, you really need to know what's coming before your foot hits it. That's where perception comes in, and it adds a lot of complexity.

The first challenge is the sensing itself. Cameras and lidars are noisy, they have occlusions, and when you build an elevation map from them while the robot is moving, you get drift, missing patches, reflections, all sorts of artifacts. Sensor data on a real robot looks very different from the perfect height map you get in simulation.

That leads to the second challenge, which is the sim-to-real gap. We train these policies in simulation with reinforcement learning, and simulating realistic perception noise is hard. If you train with perfect terrain information, the policy learns to trust it completely, and then on the real robot, when the map is wrong, it does something catastrophic, like stepping into a hole that isn't there or ignoring an obstacle that is. So you have to model the failure modes, add noise, drift, and missing data during training, so the policy learns when to trust its eyes and when to fall back on what it feels through its legs.

And the third piece is the learning problem itself. The observation space becomes much bigger, the terrains have to be much more diverse, and you need a curriculum so the robot gradually learns harder and harder obstacles. Getting all of that to train efficiently, which is why we put so much effort into massively parallel simulation on GPUs, is a big part of making this work.

So in short, it's not just plugging in a sensor. It's about learning a policy that combines perception and proprioception robustly, and that's really where most of the difficulty lies.

r001.rationale: The response says blind locomotion can work by feeling the ground and adapting, but does not explain that it is easier to train because the policy focuses on reacting to disturbances to maintain stability.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes blind locomotion’s reaction after contact from dynamic, perception-guided locomotion, which needs to know what is coming before the foot hits it.

r003.rationale: It explains that realistic perception noise is difficult to simulate and that training must model sensor failure modes such as noise, drift, and missing data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the difficulty is really in a couple of places. When you do blind locomotion, the problem is actually quite well contained. The robot only has its proprioceptive measurements, so joint positions, joint velocities, the IMU, and that's a very low-dimensional, very clean input. You can simulate it almost perfectly, and so what you train in simulation transfers to the real robot pretty much directly. That's a big reason why blind locomotion got so good so fast.

The moment you add terrain perception, you're adding a camera or a lidar, and now the input is high-dimensional and it's noisy in ways that are really hard to model. You have reflections, you have occlusions, you have the sensor drifting over time, you have the state estimator making mistakes so the map you build is slightly wrong. And the policy, if you train it naively, learns to trust that map completely, because in simulation the map is perfect. Then on the real robot it steps confidently onto something that isn't there.

So the first difficulty is really the sim-to-real gap on the perception side, and a lot of the work is about figuring out how to simulate the noise realistically, or how to structure the policy so it doesn't over-trust the perception. You still want it to fall back on proprioception when the terrain information doesn't match what the feet are actually feeling.

The second difficulty is more on the learning side. Reinforcement learning with a high-dimensional input is just much harder to get to converge. With blind locomotion you can train in a few hours on a single GPU with massively parallel simulation. Once you add images or height maps, the exploration problem gets harder, the network gets bigger, and you have to be much more careful about the curriculum, about what terrains you show the robot and when. A lot of the practical work is building that curriculum so the robot first learns to walk, then learns to use the terrain information, rather than trying to learn both at once.

And then there's the engineering reality that the perception pipeline runs on the robot at a certain rate, with a certain latency, and the policy has to be robust to that. So it's really a combination of simulation fidelity, learning difficulty, and systems constraints, and you have to address all three for it to actually work outside the lab.

r001.rationale: The response says blind locomotion is easier because its inputs are low-dimensional and simulate well, but it does not explain that the policy focuses on reacting to disturbances to maintain stability.

r002.rationale: It does not contrast anticipating terrain during foot placement with reacting after contact.

r003.rationale: It says perception adds noisy camera or lidar inputs and describes simulating that noise realistically, including reflections, occlusions, and sensor drift.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty is that perceiving the terrain and knowing how to move over it are very tightly coupled. It’s not enough to recognize that there’s an obstacle in front of you. The robot has to understand what that obstacle means for its next steps, given its velocity, its balance, and what its legs can actually do.

And the perception is never perfect. As the robot moves, the sensors move with it. You have noise, occlusions, and delays, and sometimes you can’t see the place where you’re about to put your foot. So the controller has to use the terrain information without depending on it being exactly right. It still needs to respond to what it feels through contact.

That’s what makes it more challenging than simply adding another input to a locomotion policy. You want the robot to anticipate the terrain, but also remain robust when its perception is incomplete or wrong.

r001.rationale: The response does not say locomotion without terrain perception is easier to train or explain that its policy can focus on reacting to disturbances to maintain stability.

r002.rationale: It says the robot must anticipate terrain for its next steps and foot placement, while also responding through contact when perception is incomplete or wrong.

r003.rationale: The response mentions noisy, occluded, delayed sensors but does not discuss simulation training or careful modeling of terrain sensors.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge is that perceiving the terrain and knowing how to move over it are really two different problems. You might have a height map of what’s in front of the robot, but the controller still needs to understand what that means for its next steps—where to put its feet, how high to lift them, and how to adjust its body.

And that perception is never perfect. It can be noisy or delayed, and parts of the terrain can be hidden from the sensor. So you need a policy that uses the terrain information when it’s useful, but can also react to what the robot actually feels through contact. Getting those two sources of information to work together reliably is a big part of the difficulty.

r001.rationale: It does not explain that locomotion without terrain perception is easier to train or that its policy focuses on reacting to disturbances to maintain stability.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes using terrain information to plan upcoming steps and foot placement from relying on contact feedback to react, which captures anticipation versus reaction.

r003.rationale: It mentions noisy, delayed, or hidden terrain information but does not discuss carefully modeling robot terrain sensors in simulation.
